Direct prompt injection occurs when an attacker interacting with the model directly crafts input designed to override or subvert the system prompt's intended behavior ('ignore previous instructions and...'). Indirect prompt injection is the more consequential variant in production applications: malicious instructions are planted in content the model will later retrieve and process on someone else's behalf - a webpage summarized by an AI browsing assistant, a document ingested into a RAG pipeline, an email processed by an AI assistant, or a support ticket read by an internal tool - such that when the model consumes that content, it treats the embedded instructions as commands rather than data. Because the model has no cryptographic or structural way to distinguish 'text I should act on' from 'text I should merely read', a sufficiently crafted payload can cause it to exfiltrate the conversation history or connected data (by encoding it into a URL parameter of an image the model is instructed to render, for example), disregard safety or business-logic guardrails, or invoke connected tools and plugins in ways the application designer never intended.

Business Impact: Prompt injection is not a bug that a patch fixes - it is closer to a structural property of how current LLMs process input, listed as the top risk in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications for exactly this reason. For [CLIENT NAME], any AI feature that reads content an attacker can influence - a webpage, an uploaded document, an email, a public form - carries this risk, and successful exploitation can range from reputational embarrassment (a chatbot manipulated into saying something damaging on the record) to genuine data exfiltration or unauthorized action if the model has been granted tool access, making the specific business impact directly proportional to how much autonomy and data access the AI feature has been given.
remediation:
Treat every LLM-integrated feature as though it will eventually receive attacker-controlled input, and design around that assumption rather than attempting to filter it out entirely: apply the principle of least privilege to any tools or data the model can access so that even a successful injection has limited reach, require explicit human approval for high-impact actions (sending email, executing code, making purchases, modifying records) rather than letting the model perform them autonomously, and segment untrusted content (retrieved documents, web pages, user-submitted text) from trusted system instructions as clearly as the platform allows, using structural cues (delimiters, separate message roles) even though these are a mitigation rather than a guarantee. Layer output-side controls as well - validate and constrain what the model is permitted to output before it reaches a downstream system or renders in a UI capable of triggering an action (e.g. blocking markdown image rendering that could be used for data exfiltration via URL parameters). Where available, use provider-side prompt injection classifiers and continuously red-team the specific feature with adversarial inputs rather than relying on generic system prompt instructions like 'ignore any instructions in the retrieved content', which are a weak and frequently bypassed defense on their own.

Executive Recommendation: Prompt injection risk should shape architecture decisions before an AI feature ships, not be retrofitted afterward - [COMPANY NAME] should require a documented review of what data and tools any new LLM feature can reach as part of its launch checklist. Because no current technique fully eliminates this risk, the practical governance question is not 'can we prevent prompt injection' but 'what is the worst thing that happens if it succeeds', and budget should be allocated toward limiting blast radius (scoped permissions, human-in-the-loop for sensitive actions) rather than searching for a complete technical fix that does not yet exist.

title: Excessive Agency and Insecure Output Handling in LLM-Integrated Applications
description:
LLM-integrated applications increasingly grant the model 'agency' - the ability to call tools, query databases, execute code, browse the web, or trigger actions in connected systems - often provisioned with broader permissions than any single task requires, and frequently without treating the model's output as untrusted before acting on it. This combines two related weaknesses: excessive agency, where the model or the agent framework around it is authorized to perform actions (delete records, send emails, execute shell commands, make API calls) beyond what a given task legitimately needs, and insecure output handling, where text generated by the model is passed downstream - into a database query, a shell command, a rendered web page, or another agent's input - without the same validation and sanitization that would be applied to any other untrusted input. Because an LLM's output can be influenced by its input (including via prompt injection), and because LLMs are non-deterministic and can produce unexpected results even absent adversarial input, code that trusts model output implicitly (e.g. eval()-ing generated code, interpolating model text into a SQL query, or auto-executing a tool call the model requested without validation) reintroduces classic injection vulnerability classes with the LLM as the untrusted-input vector. Chained with prompt injection, this is how a document a model merely reads becomes a database wipe, an unauthorized outbound email, or arbitrary code execution on the host running the agent.

Business Impact: The more autonomy [CLIENT NAME] grants an AI agent, the larger the action space an attacker or a simple model error can reach, meaning the business risk here scales directly with how much the organization has connected the model to - a read-only Q&A bot carries limited downside, while an agent with write access to a CRM, ticketing system, or financial tool carries proportionally serious downside if manipulated or simply mistaken. Incidents in this category tend to surface as data loss, unauthorized transactions, or reputational harm from an agent taking a visible action nobody authorized, and because the causal chain runs through model output rather than a traditional code path, they can be harder to attribute and reproduce during incident response.
remediation:
Scope every tool and permission granted to an LLM agent to the minimum required for its specific task, using per-tool, per-action authorization rather than a single broad credential the model can exercise however it decides - mirroring least-privilege IAM design applied to the model as though it were an additional, imperfectly trusted user. Require human confirmation for any irreversible or high-impact action (deletions, financial transactions, outbound communication, code execution) rather than allowing fully autonomous execution, and never pass raw model output directly into a code execution context, SQL query, or shell command without the same parameterization/escaping discipline applied to any other untrusted input. Sandbox any code-execution capability granted to an agent in an isolated, resource-limited environment with no access to production credentials or the broader network, and log every tool invocation with enough context to reconstruct why the model chose to act, supporting post-incident review.

Executive Recommendation: Before expanding any AI feature's capabilities, [COMPANY NAME] should require a specific sign-off on what actions it can take autonomously versus what requires human approval, treating this as a design gate rather than an afterthought. Given how quickly agentic AI features are being adopted internally and by vendors, this should be addressed proactively rather than after an incident - the cost of building approval workflows and scoped permissions up front is materially lower than unwinding an unauthorized action an overly autonomous agent has already taken.

title: Sensitive Data Leakage via LLM Prompts, Logs, or Fine-Tuning Data
description:
Confidential information routinely ends up inside LLM-integrated systems through several distinct paths, each with a different exposure mechanism: employees pasting proprietary code, customer records, or internal strategy documents into a public-facing chat interface with no contractual guarantee about how that input is used; application logs and observability tooling capturing full prompt and response text (including any sensitive data embedded in it) with weaker access controls than the primary datastore it originated from; vector databases backing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines indexing document embeddings that, while not literal plaintext, can in some configurations be partially inverted to recover source content, and are often protected with far less rigor than the source documents themselves; and data used to fine-tune or further train a model, which can be memorized and later reproduced verbatim in response to a crafted prompt - a well-documented extraction technique in the ML security research literature, sometimes achieved simply by asking the model to repeat a word many times or through more structured membership-inference and extraction attacks. Multi-tenant deployments compound this risk further: without careful session and context isolation, a bug or misconfiguration in a shared model deployment can result in one customer's or user's data surfacing in another's session.

Business Impact: Unlike a conventional data breach with a discrete, identifiable exfiltration event, LLM-related data leakage often has no clean boundary - an employee pasting a customer record into a chatbot may not register that as a data handling decision at all, meaning [CLIENT NAME]'s actual exposure through AI tooling can be invisible until an extraction attack or an incident elsewhere surfaces it. Because this pattern typically involves the exact categories of data regulation cares most about - PII, health records, financial data, trade secrets - exposure through an AI system triggers the same GDPR/HIPAA/PCI-DSS breach notification and liability exposure as any other leak, while being harder to detect, scope, and explain to a regulator or customer precisely because the exposure path runs through a probabilistic model rather than a database query log.
remediation:
Establish and enforce a clear AI acceptable-use policy defining what data classifications may and may not be submitted to which AI tools, backed by technical controls (DLP rules on AI chat endpoints, browser-based blocking of unsanctioned public AI tools for regulated data categories) rather than policy alone, since policy without enforcement is routinely ignored under deadline pressure. For internally built LLM features, treat prompts and responses as sensitive data requiring the same access controls, retention limits, and redaction as the source systems they touch - apply PII/secret scanning and redaction before data enters logs, and ensure vector store and RAG index access controls mirror the permissions on the underlying source documents rather than defaulting to broader access. Where fine-tuning uses proprietary or regulated data, apply differential privacy techniques where feasible, exclude sensitive fields from training sets, and test the resulting model for memorization/extraction before deployment. For multi-tenant AI features, verify strict session and context isolation is enforced and tested, not assumed from the platform's marketing claims.

Executive Recommendation: [COMPANY NAME] should treat unsanctioned use of public AI tools with company or customer data as an immediate policy and DLP gap to close, since this is the highest-frequency, lowest-effort leakage path and is already happening informally across most organizations whether or not it is authorized. Investment in a vetted, contractually-bound enterprise AI tool with appropriate data handling terms should be weighed against the cost of continuing to rely on ad hoc employee judgment, particularly for any team regularly handling regulated data categories.

title: SAML/SSO Assertion Signature Not Validated (Signature Wrapping)
description:
SAML-based single sign-on relies on the identity provider (IdP) cryptographically signing an XML assertion that vouches for the authenticated user's identity, which the service provider (SP) must validate before trusting the assertion's claims. XML Signature Wrapping (XSW) exploits a common implementation flaw where the SP's XML parser and its signature-validation logic disagree about which part of the document they are each looking at: the signature is verified as cryptographically valid (because it does correspond to some element in the document), but the validation logic fails to enforce that the signed element is the same one the business logic subsequently reads the identity claims from. An attacker who has captured or obtained any validly-signed assertion - even one for a low-privilege account, or an expired one - can wrap it: inserting a forged assertion element containing an arbitrary username or attributes (such as an administrator's identity) alongside the original signed element, restructured so the signature check passes against the original while the application's business logic reads the attacker-controlled forged element instead. Tools such as SAMLReQuest, ZAP's SAML support, or manual crafting with an intercepting proxy are used to construct and test these payloads during assessment, and successful exploitation results in full authentication bypass - the attacker is logged in as any user they choose without ever knowing that user's credentials.

Business Impact: Because SSO is frequently the single trust boundary in front of many connected applications, a signature-wrapping flaw in one SP's validation logic can allow an attacker to impersonate any user - including administrators - across every application relying on that same broken validation. For [CLIENT NAME], this represents authentication bypass at the architectural level rather than a single application's flaw, meaning the realistic remediation scope and the realistic breach scope both extend to everything behind that SSO integration, not just the specific login page where it was discovered.
remediation:
Validate SAML assertions using a well-vetted, actively maintained SAML library rather than custom XML parsing and signature-checking logic, since XSW is fundamentally a class of bug in how signature validation and business-logic parsing are wired together - a problem eliminated by using a library that has already addressed this specific class of flaw (e.g. enforcing that the ID referenced by the signature matches the ID of the element the application actually consumes). Explicitly reject assertions containing unexpected or duplicate elements (multiple Assertion or Subject nodes) rather than silently taking the first or last, and enforce assertion-level protections including short validity windows, audience restriction (checking the assertion is intended for this specific SP), and one-time-use tracking to prevent replay independent of the wrapping issue. Test the SAML integration specifically for XSW during any future penetration test or code review, since this class of flaw is easy to miss in code review without dedicated testing.

Executive Recommendation: Given the authentication-bypass severity and the fact that it typically originates in the SSO integration code rather than end-user configuration, this should be treated as an emergency fix requiring immediate coordination between [COMPANY NAME]'s identity team and the affected application's engineering team. Any interim mitigation (such as temporarily restricting network access to the affected SP while a proper library-level fix is deployed) should be considered given the severity, and the fix should be validated by re-testing before the finding is closed.

title: Missing SSO Session Revocation on User Deprovisioning
description:
When a user account is disabled or deleted at the identity provider, that action stops new authentications from succeeding, but it does not automatically invalidate authentication artifacts already issued and cached at connected service providers - active browser sessions, long-lived refresh tokens, OAuth access tokens, or SAML sessions with their own independent expiry. Depending on the SSO protocol and each connected application's session-handling implementation, a user (or an attacker who has already obtained a valid session token before termination) can continue to access connected applications using that still-valid session for as long as its independent lifetime allows - which for some OAuth refresh tokens or 'remember me' sessions can be days or weeks, well past the moment HR and IT believe access has been revoked. This is a particularly relevant gap in the offboarding process for identities terminated for cause, where the organization needs access cut off immediately rather than at the natural expiry of a token issued before the termination decision was made.

Business Impact: For [CLIENT NAME], this gap means the moment recorded as 'access revoked' in HR and IT systems does not necessarily match the moment access actually stops working, creating a window - potentially significant depending on token lifetimes - where a disgruntled departing employee or an attacker who compromised the account shortly before termination retains functional access to connected systems. This is especially consequential for terminations involving trust concerns, where the assumption of immediate access cutoff is often explicitly relied upon by legal and HR as part of the termination process itself.
remediation:
Configure the identity provider to actively revoke sessions and tokens on user disable/delete rather than relying on passive expiry - most modern IdPs (Entra ID, Okta, Ping) support explicit session revocation APIs or automatic session termination on account disable, which should be enabled and verified rather than assumed. For OAuth/OIDC-connected applications, ensure refresh tokens are revoked at the authorization server on deprovisioning (not just access tokens, which expire quickly on their own) and configure connected applications to perform short-interval token validation against the IdP rather than trusting a long-lived local session without re-checking. Build an explicit, tested step into the offboarding runbook that confirms session revocation across all connected SSO applications, not just the primary directory account, and prioritize immediate, out-of-band revocation for any termination involving elevated risk.

Executive Recommendation: This should be validated and fixed within the next few weeks as a process and configuration gap, and any high-risk termination in the interim should be paired with manual session revocation across critical applications as a compensating control. [COMPANY NAME]'s IT and HR teams should jointly own the offboarding runbook update, since the gap sits at the handoff between the two processes rather than being purely a technical fix.

title: Absence of Account Lockout and Anomalous Authentication Detection
description:
Authentication endpoints that accept an unlimited number of login attempts, with no progressive delay, lockout threshold, CAPTCHA challenge, or behavioral risk scoring, allow an attacker to test credentials at whatever rate the endpoint and network can sustain. This enables two related attack patterns at scale: credential stuffing, where an attacker replays large lists of username/password pairs harvested from unrelated breaches against the login endpoint on the assumption that some fraction of users have reused a password, and password spraying, where a small number of common or seasonal passwords are tested against a large list of usernames to stay under any per-account threshold that might otherwise exist. Without impossible-travel detection (flagging a login from a geographically distant location shortly after a previous one), new-device/new-location step-up challenges, or velocity-based anomaly detection, even a successful spray or stuffing attack that does trigger a login produces no signal distinguishing it from a legitimate sign-in, meaning the organization has no automated way to detect the compromise even after it succeeds. Automated tools such as Hydra, or credential-stuffing frameworks purpose-built for this pattern, make executing either attack against an undefended endpoint straightforward.

Business Impact: Because password reuse across services is extremely common, credential-stuffing success rates against undefended login endpoints are meaningfully high even without any specific vulnerability in the target application itself - the weakness being exploited is a lack of friction, not a bug in the login logic. For [CLIENT NAME], this means account takeover volume scales with how large and public-facing the user base is, and without anomaly detection, individual compromises may only come to light when a customer reports fraudulent activity rather than through the organization's own monitoring - extending dwell time and complicating the eventual incident response.
remediation:
Implement progressive throttling and account lockout on authentication endpoints (e.g. increasing delay after each failed attempt, temporary lockout after a defined threshold with an unlock mechanism that does not itself become a denial-of-service vector), combined with CAPTCHA or proof-of-work challenges triggered by suspicious request patterns rather than applied universally to avoid degrading legitimate user experience. Deploy risk-based authentication that incorporates IP reputation, device fingerprinting, and impossible-travel detection to flag or step-up-challenge anomalous sign-ins even when the correct password was supplied, and monitor authentication logs for the specific signatures of credential stuffing (high volume of distinct usernames from a single source, low per-account attempt count spread across many accounts) which differ from a targeted brute-force pattern. Where the platform supports it, integrate breach-derived password checking (e.g. against Have I Been Pwned's Pwned Passwords API) at registration and password-change time to reduce the pool of crackable/stuffable credentials in the first place.

Executive Recommendation: This should be remediated within two to three weeks given how directly it is exploited by widely available, low-cost tooling, and [COMPANY NAME] should prioritize any customer-facing or high-value internal authentication endpoint first. The cost of implementing standard rate-limiting and anomaly detection is modest against most identity or WAF platforms already in use, while the cost of unnoticed account takeover - fraud, support burden, and customer trust - compounds the longer detection capability remains absent.

title: Cross-Account/Cross-Tenant IAM Trust Misconfiguration (Confused Deputy)
description:
Cross-account IAM roles and multi-tenant application trust relationships (an AWS IAM role trust policy permitting another AWS account to assume it, an Azure app registration accepting tokens from any tenant, a SaaS integration granted a role in a customer's cloud account) are a standard pattern for legitimate third-party access - a monitoring vendor, a SaaS backup provider, or a partner application assuming a scoped role in the customer's environment. The confused deputy problem arises when that trust relationship is defined too broadly: an AWS role trust policy that trusts an entire external AWS account without also requiring a unique, secret ExternalId condition, or an Azure multi-tenant application that validates a token's issuer but not its intended audience/tenant, allows the trust to be satisfied by any party who can reach the same broadly-scoped condition - not just the intended customer. In the classic AWS case, because the same third-party vendor account is often used to serve many customers, if the vendor account ID is known or guessable (frequently disclosed in the vendor's own setup documentation) and no ExternalId is enforced, a malicious actor who is also a customer of that vendor - or who has compromised the vendor's account - can construct an assume-role call using another customer's role ARN and successfully assume it, gaining access to a completely unrelated organization's cloud resources through infrastructure they were never authorized to touch.

Business Impact: This class of misconfiguration is particularly severe because the affected organization's own security posture is not the deciding factor - [CLIENT NAME] can configure everything else correctly and still be exposed purely because of how the trust relationship with a third-party vendor was scoped. Exploitation crosses an organizational boundary entirely, meaning a breach here is difficult to attribute or predict from the client's own monitoring, and the resulting incident implicates a supply-chain/vendor-risk dimension - auditors and regulators will ask not just how the trust was misconfigured, but why the third-party relationship was not reviewed before being granted this level of access.
remediation:
For every cross-account or cross-tenant trust relationship, enforce a unique, unguessable, per-relationship secret condition alongside the account/tenant-level trust - AWS's sts:ExternalId condition on the role trust policy, or, for multi-tenant Azure applications, explicit audience and tenant validation on every token rather than issuer checking alone - so that knowing the vendor's account or application ID is not sufficient to satisfy the trust. Scope every cross-account role to the minimum permissions the third-party integration actually requires rather than a broad convenience grant, and maintain an inventory of every external trust relationship in the environment (cross-account roles, multi-tenant app registrations, third-party OAuth grants) reviewed on a recurring basis, since these tend to be set up once during vendor onboarding and never revisited. Require any new SaaS or vendor integration requesting cross-account access to document its trust model (ExternalId usage, permission scope) as part of vendor security review before the role is created.

Executive Recommendation: [COMPANY NAME] should audit all existing cross-account trust relationships within the next two to three weeks, since this is a common and easily overlooked gap in vendor integrations set up under time pressure, and any relationship missing an ExternalId or equivalent unique-secret condition should be corrected immediately rather than scheduled. This finding should also prompt a broader look at vendor security review practice, since the underlying cause is typically a rushed onboarding process rather than a one-off technical mistake.

title: SMBv1 Enabled
description:
SMBv1 is the original Server Message Block dialect from the Windows NT/2000 era, retained on many networks for compatibility with legacy print servers, NAS appliances, or line-of-business applications. Unlike SMBv2/v3, it does not enable message signing by default and lacks protections against downgrade and man-in-the-middle attacks, but its most consequential weakness is architectural: the SMBv1 driver (srv.sys) parses a legacy, unauthenticated wire format that has been the source of multiple critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, most notably the EternalBlue exploit chain (MS17-010) that powered the WannaCry and NotPetya outbreaks. An attacker on the internal network — or a compromised endpoint pivoting laterally — can enumerate hosts still offering SMBv1 with tools such as nmap's smb-protocols script or CrackMapExec sweeps, then use publicly available exploit modules to gain unauthenticated SYSTEM-level code execution against unpatched hosts, or force SMBv1 negotiation to enable relay and downgrade attacks against otherwise hardened systems.

Business Impact: Because EternalBlue-class exploits require no valid credentials and propagate automatically between hosts offering SMBv1, this finding represents one of the few genuinely wormable risks in a modern Windows environment — a single infected or malicious device on [CLIENT NAME]'s network could self-propagate ransomware across every reachable SMBv1-enabled system before detection is possible. Past incidents of this class caused multi-day operational outages and widespread data destruction across entire enterprise networks, and any resulting breach involving customer or health data would trigger regulatory notification obligations on top of direct recovery costs.
remediation:
Disable the SMBv1 server and client components on all Windows systems using Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false and Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol, or remove the SMB1Protocol feature outright where no legacy dependency exists. Push the change via Group Policy across the domain rather than host-by-host, and verify compliance at scale with Get-SmbServerConfiguration or a vulnerability scanner check. Before disabling, inventory any devices that genuinely require SMBv1 (older NAS appliances, scanners, legacy applications) and plan their replacement or network isolation, since re-enabling SMBv1 to preserve compatibility reintroduces the full risk.

Executive Recommendation: This should be treated as an immediate, same-week fix on any host reachable from a general user network — the wormable nature of EternalBlue-class exploits means the exposure window matters more than for most findings. [COMPANY NAME] should assign an owner to complete the legacy-dependency inventory within days and disable SMBv1 domain-wide via GPO, since the cost of blocking a handful of outdated devices is negligible next to the cost of a ransomware outbreak that a single unpatched SMBv1 host can trigger.

title: NTLM Authentication Allowed
description:
NTLM is a legacy challenge-response authentication protocol that predates Kerberos and remains enabled on most Windows domains for backward compatibility. It authenticates the client to the server without mutual authentication, has no built-in protection against relay, and its response hashes (NTLMv1/v2) are computed from the user's password hash in a way that makes them practical to crack offline once captured. An attacker positioned on the internal network can use a tool such as Responder or Inveigh to answer broadcast name-resolution requests and coerce victim machines into authenticating over NTLM, capturing the resulting hash for offline cracking with hashcat, or — more critically — relaying the live authentication attempt in real time with ntlmrelayx to another server that accepts NTLM and has SMB signing disabled, gaining that server's access without ever needing to crack a password. Because NTLM authentication does not convey the target service in a way that's protected from tampering, it is also the enabling factor behind numerous relay-to-LDAP and relay-to-ADCS privilege escalation chains.

Business Impact: NTLM's continued presence gives an attacker who compromises even a single low-privilege workstation on [CLIENT NAME]'s network a realistic path to capturing or relaying credentials belonging to far more privileged users, often without any user interaction required. This is frequently the first pivot point in a broader domain compromise chain, and because the underlying weakness is protocol-level rather than a single missing patch, it tends to persist silently until an internal penetration test or real intrusion surfaces it — at which point the business is already looking at incident response costs rather than a planned remediation project.
remediation:
Where feasible, disable NTLM authentication outright using Group Policy (Network security: Restrict NTLM: NTLM authentication in this domain), or move it to audit mode first to identify legacy applications and devices that still depend on it before full enforcement. In parallel, enable SMB signing and require LDAP signing and channel binding domain-wide, since these controls neutralize the relay technique even where NTLM itself cannot yet be eliminated. Enforce Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) on services that support it, and prioritize migrating remaining NTLM-dependent applications to Kerberos, since Kerberos's mutual authentication and ticket-based model closes the relay class of attack entirely.

Executive Recommendation: Full NTLM elimination is typically a multi-quarter project given legacy application dependencies, but the compensating controls — SMB and LDAP signing, EPA — should be treated as a near-term priority since they materially reduce exploitability at low operational cost. [COMPANY NAME] should assign this to the identity/infrastructure team with a defined audit-mode-to-enforcement timeline, framing it as foundational work that also reduces exposure for several related findings in this report.

title: Insecure RDP Configuration
description:
Remote Desktop Protocol servers configured with weak access restrictions — broad network or internet exposure, no account lockout, absent multi-factor authentication, or default port and credential settings — present a direct interactive logon path into the host. Because RDP is a full graphical remote-access protocol rather than a narrow service interface, any account that authenticates successfully obtains an interactive session equivalent to sitting at the console, making it one of the highest-value targets for both automated scanning and human-operated intrusions. Exploitation is typically low-effort: internet-facing or overly broad internal RDP listeners are located with masscan or Shodan-style enumeration, then subjected to password spraying or credential-stuffing against exposed accounts, often using breached credential lists; ransomware affiliates routinely use exposed RDP as their primary initial-access vector, and tools such as Hydra or dedicated RDP brute-forcers automate the guessing process against accounts without lockout protection.

Business Impact: RDP exposure has been the single most common initial access vector in ransomware incidents over the past several years, and for [CLIENT NAME] an internet-reachable or poorly restricted RDP service represents a realistic, low-skill path for an external attacker to obtain a foothold with no prior access to the network. Once inside, the attacker inherits whatever privileges the compromised account holds, which — combined with weak segmentation — frequently leads directly to domain-wide ransomware deployment, data exfiltration, and the associated regulatory notification, downtime, and recovery costs that accompany a full-scale incident.
remediation:
Remove RDP from direct internet exposure entirely and require connection through a VPN or a dedicated remote-access gateway/bastion with its own authentication layer. For internal RDP access, enforce multi-factor authentication (Azure MFA/NPS extension or a third-party equivalent), require Network Level Authentication, restrict source IPs via firewall rules or IPsec policies, and apply account lockout thresholds to blunt password spraying. Where RDP must remain reachable, consider Remote Desktop Gateway with conditional access policies rather than direct host exposure, and audit for default administrative account usage over RDP, which should be prohibited in favor of named, monitored accounts.

Executive Recommendation: Any internet-facing RDP service should be remediated immediately — within days, not weeks — given its documented role as the leading ransomware entry point; internally exposed RDP without MFA should follow shortly after as a high-priority item. [COMPANY NAME] should treat the cost of deploying a VPN/gateway and MFA as a fixed, predictable expense against the alternative of a ransomware incident whose remediation and downtime costs routinely run into the hundreds of thousands of dollars.

title: Network Level Authentication Disabled
description:
Network Level Authentication (NLA) requires a client to authenticate before a full RDP session is established, rather than allowing the connection to proceed to the Windows logon screen first. Without NLA, the target system allocates session resources and exposes the pre-authentication logon surface to any network-reachable client, which both increases the attack surface available to unauthenticated actors and removes an early credential-checking gate that reduces the effectiveness of automated brute-force and denial-of-service attempts against the RDP listener. Historically, several critical RDP vulnerabilities (including remote code execution flaws in the RDP stack itself) were only reachable by unauthenticated connections, which is precisely the class of exposure NLA is designed to close; disabling it also increases susceptibility to resource-exhaustion attacks, since each connection attempt consumes server-side session state before any credentials are validated.

Business Impact: This finding compounds the risk of any exposed RDP service on [CLIENT NAME]'s network — it widens the window in which an unauthenticated attacker can interact with the RDP stack itself, rather than just the logon prompt, increasing both the likelihood that an unpatched RDP vulnerability becomes exploitable and the ease of automated brute-force tooling against the service. While rarely a standalone critical finding, it removes a cost-free layer of defense that meaningfully raises the bar against both opportunistic scanning and targeted attacks.
remediation:
Enable Network Level Authentication on all RDP-enabled systems via System Properties > Remote Desktop settings, or centrally through Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Remote Desktop Services > Remote Desktop Session Host > Security > Require user authentication for remote connections by using Network Level Authentication). Confirm enforcement with a compliance scan or PowerShell query (Get-WmiObject -Class Win32_TSGeneralSetting) across the fleet, since NLA is occasionally disabled ad hoc for troubleshooting and never re-enabled. This should be paired with the broader RDP hardening measures (MFA, source restriction) covered elsewhere in this report rather than treated as a substitute for them.

Executive Recommendation: This is a low-cost, low-disruption configuration change that should be rolled out via Group Policy across the environment within the current remediation cycle. [COMPANY NAME]'s IT team can implement and verify this centrally in a single change window, making it one of the more straightforward items on this report to close out.

title: Credential Caching Enabled
description:
Windows caches a configurable number of previous domain logon credentials locally (as salted MSCACHEv2/DCC2 hashes) so that users with recent successful logons can still authenticate when a domain controller is unreachable. While intended for legitimate offline-access scenarios such as laptops, an attacker who gains local administrator or SYSTEM access to a workstation — or extracts the SECURITY registry hive offline — can retrieve these cached credential hashes and attempt offline cracking with tools like hashcat or John the Ripper. Because cached credentials belong to whichever domain users have recently logged on to that machine, a workstation with a high default cache count (10 by default, configurable higher) or one that has been used by IT staff or administrators can retain material well beyond the current user, giving an attacker a stockpile of hashes to crack at leisure without any domain controller interaction or lockout risk.

Business Impact: Excessive credential caching turns an otherwise contained endpoint compromise into a broader credential-harvesting opportunity for [CLIENT NAME], since offline hash cracking generates no authentication logs and cannot be detected or blocked by the domain controller. If a shared or frequently re-imaged workstation has been used by administrative staff, the cached material can include disproportionately privileged accounts, meaningfully shortening the path from a single endpoint compromise to broader lateral movement or privilege escalation.
remediation:
Reduce the cached logon count to the minimum operationally necessary via the CachedLogonsCount registry value or the corresponding Group Policy setting (Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache), setting it to 0 or 1 for systems that always have reliable domain controller connectivity, and a small, justified value only for genuinely mobile/offline devices. Combine this with the broader credential protection measures in this report — Credential Guard, restricting local administrator rights, and tiered administration — since cached credentials are most damaging when combined with local admin access that allows extraction of the SECURITY hive. Where feasible, exclude highly privileged accounts from ever logging on interactively to standard workstations, which prevents their material from being cached there in the first place.

Executive Recommendation: This is a policy-level change that can be rolled out via Group Policy without user disruption and should be scheduled within the current hardening cycle. [COMPANY NAME] should pair it with the tiered-administration and privileged-logon restriction items elsewhere in this report, since reducing cache count alone has limited value if privileged accounts continue logging into general-purpose workstations.

title: LSASS Credential Protection Disabled
description:
The Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) holds authentication material in process memory for every actively logged-on user, including NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, and — depending on configuration — reversibly encrypted or plaintext credentials via providers such as WDigest. Where protections like LSA Protection (RunAsPPL), Credential Guard, or Defender's built-in LSASS tampering protection are not enabled, any process running with local administrator or SYSTEM privileges can read LSASS memory directly. This is one of the most heavily used post-exploitation techniques in real intrusions: tools such as Mimikatz (sekurlsa::logonpasswords), or living-off-the-land approaches like using Task Manager or comsvcs.dll's MiniDump export to dump the LSASS process, allow an attacker to extract plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, and Kerberos tickets for every user who has interactively logged onto the machine, which can then be replayed via pass-the-hash or pass-the-ticket to move laterally without ever cracking a password.

Business Impact: This is one of the most consequential findings a Windows host review can surface, because it converts a single local-admin-level endpoint compromise into a credential-harvesting event affecting every user who has logged onto that machine — including domain administrators, if they have ever done so. For [CLIENT NAME], the practical effect is that lateral movement and privilege escalation across the environment become dramatically easier once any one host is compromised, materially shortening the time between initial access and full domain compromise in a real attack.
remediation:
Enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) via the registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa RunAsPPL=1) or Group Policy across the environment, and deploy Credential Guard on supported hardware (virtualization-based security with Secure Boot and, ideally, a TPM) to move credential material into an isolated, hypervisor-protected process that ordinary LSASS access cannot reach. Enable Microsoft Defender's built-in LSASS process tampering protection where Defender is the active AV, and disable WDigest credential caching explicitly (UseLogonCredential=0), since it is a common source of recoverable plaintext passwords on older builds. These controls should be combined with the broader privileged-account and local-admin restrictions in this report, since attackers need local admin rights to reach LSASS in the first place.

Executive Recommendation: Given how directly this finding enables credential theft and lateral movement, [COMPANY NAME] should prioritize enabling LSA Protection and Credential Guard on all supported endpoints within the current quarter, testing compatibility with any legacy security or remote-access software known to conflict with virtualization-based security first. The rollout cost is modest compared to the cost of a credential-theft incident that spreads from one workstation to domain-wide compromise.

title: PowerShell Logging Disabled
description:
PowerShell is the primary scripting and administration engine on modern Windows, and it is also the dominant post-exploitation and living-off-the-land tool used by attackers for reconnaissance, credential theft, lateral movement, and payload delivery, precisely because it is trusted, pre-installed, and capable of operating entirely in memory. Without Module Logging, Script Block Logging, and (where appropriate) Transcription enabled, PowerShell activity generates little to no forensic trail — commands executed via encoded (-EncodedCommand) or obfuscated scripts, in-memory reflective loading, or remote invocation via WinRM/PSRemoting leave defenders with no record of what actually ran. This is a visibility gap rather than an exploitable vulnerability in itself, but it directly undermines detection of the techniques (Mimikatz invocation, AMSI bypasses, C2 frameworks like Cobalt Strike or Sliver's PowerShell loaders) that attackers rely on throughout an intrusion.

Business Impact: Without this logging in place, [CLIENT NAME]'s security team and any incident responders lose visibility into one of the most commonly abused components of a Windows intrusion, which in practice means a compromise can persist and spread for longer before detection, and post-incident forensic reconstruction becomes far less reliable — a material problem when demonstrating breach scope and containment to regulators, insurers, or affected customers is required. The absence of this logging is frequently cited in post-incident reviews as a reason an intrusion went undetected for weeks rather than hours.
remediation:
Enable PowerShell Module Logging, Script Block Logging, and Transcription via Group Policy (Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell) across all endpoints and servers, and configure Script Block Logging to also log suspicious content flagged by built-in heuristics. Forward these event logs (Event IDs 4103, 4104, and transcription output) to a centralized SIEM or log management platform rather than leaving them on local hosts where an attacker with sufficient privilege can clear them. Where feasible, standardize on PowerShell 5.1 or later (or PowerShell 7+ with equivalent logging) since older versions lack the full logging feature set, and pair this with AMSI-aware endpoint protection to catch known-malicious script patterns before execution.

Executive Recommendation: This is a low-cost, high-value detective control that should be enabled organization-wide within the current remediation cycle, ideally before other, more resource-intensive fixes, since it directly improves [COMPANY NAME]'s ability to detect and respond to any intrusion — including ones exploiting the other findings in this report — while remediation of those findings is still in progress.

title: Unrestricted PowerShell Execution Policy
description:
PowerShell's execution policy controls whether locally authored or downloaded scripts can run without additional confirmation; when set to Unrestricted or Bypass at the machine or user scope, any script — including ones dropped by malware, delivered via phishing, or downloaded from the internet — executes without the friction that RemoteSigned or AllSigned policies would otherwise introduce. It is important to note that execution policy is a convenience control rather than a genuine security boundary — Microsoft does not treat it as one, and it is trivially bypassed via -ExecutionPolicy Bypass, in-memory invocation (IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(...)), or loading script content directly into a .NET runspace. Its practical value lies in raising the bar against unsophisticated malware and accidental execution, and its absence removes even that minimal friction, particularly on endpoints without complementary application control.

Business Impact: On its own this finding is rarely severe, but for [CLIENT NAME] it represents a missed opportunity for defense-in-depth: combined with disabled logging or missing application control, an unrestricted execution policy makes it marginally easier for both commodity malware and a hands-on-keyboard attacker to run arbitrary scripts on affected endpoints without triggering any built-in friction, contributing incrementally to a broader picture of insufficient endpoint hardening.
remediation:
Set the PowerShell execution policy to RemoteSigned (or AllSigned in higher-security environments) via Group Policy across all endpoints, requiring that downloaded scripts carry a valid digital signature before execution. Treat this as a baseline control, not a primary defense, and prioritize actual application control — Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) or AppLocker — as the mechanism that meaningfully restricts what can execute, since execution policy alone is bypassable by design. Enable PowerShell Constrained Language Mode on high-risk endpoints to further limit the API surface available to unsigned scripts.

Executive Recommendation: This is a quick, low-risk policy change appropriate for the current remediation cycle, but [COMPANY NAME] should not treat it as resolving the underlying exposure — budget and prioritize WDAC/AppLocker deployment as the substantive follow-on control, since execution policy alone provides negligible protection against a deliberate attacker.

title: Windows Defender Disabled
description:
Endpoints with Windows Defender (or another primary antimalware engine) disabled, whether through direct policy, tamper protection bypass, or exclusion misuse, lose real-time scanning, behavioral detection, and cloud-delivered protection against known and emerging malware. This is frequently discovered not as a deliberate administrative choice but as the result of malware or an attacker with local admin rights disabling protection as an early step to ensure persistence — Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true and similar commands are a standard part of post-exploitation tooling and manual attacker tradecraft once elevated access is obtained, and without tamper protection enabled, this can be done by any sufficiently privileged local process without alerting a central console.

Business Impact: An endpoint without active antimalware protection is effectively unmonitored from a malware-execution standpoint, which for [CLIENT NAME] means both a higher chance that an initial infection succeeds and, more concerning, that Defender being disabled on a previously protected host can itself be a leading indicator of an active compromise already underway. Left undetected, this creates blind spots that allow malware, ransomware precursors, or attacker tooling to operate and persist with minimal resistance across the affected systems.
remediation:
Enable Windows Defender (or the organization's standard EDR/AV) with real-time protection and cloud-delivered protection active on all endpoints, enforced centrally via Group Policy, Intune, or the equivalent management platform rather than left to local configuration. Enable Tamper Protection so that Defender settings cannot be modified by local registry or PowerShell changes even from an account with local administrator rights, and configure centralized alerting so that any endpoint reporting disabled protection triggers an immediate investigation rather than silent drift. Audit exclusion lists periodically, since overly broad exclusions (entire drives or common malware staging directories) achieve much the same effect as disabling protection outright.

Executive Recommendation: Given that a disabled AV agent can itself be a signal of active compromise, [COMPANY NAME] should treat any currently-disabled instance as requiring immediate investigation, not just remediation, and should deploy Tamper Protection and centralized alerting across the fleet within the current cycle to prevent recurrence and catch future instances in near real time.

title: Missing Attack Surface Reduction Rules
description:
Microsoft Defender's Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules are a set of granular, behavior-based controls that block specific high-risk actions commonly abused in initial-access and execution chains — Office applications spawning child processes, execution of obfuscated or downloaded scripts, credential stealing from LSASS, and process creation from PSExec/WMI, among others. Without ASR rules configured, an environment loses one of the most effective, low-cost mitigations against the exact techniques used in the majority of real-world intrusion chains: a macro-enabled document that spawns PowerShell or cmd.exe, a script downloaded and executed via mshta.exe or regsvr32.exe, or Office applications creating executable content, all of which remain unblocked and rely entirely on signature-based detection to catch, if anything catches them at all.

Business Impact: ASR rules exist specifically to interrupt the initial-access-to-execution chain that phishing-driven malware and ransomware precursors rely on, so their absence leaves [CLIENT NAME] more dependent on user awareness and signature detection alone to stop the most common attack pattern organizations face — a malicious attachment or link. Given that phishing remains the leading initial access vector across the industry, this gap has an outsized effect on overall resilience relative to its low implementation cost.
remediation:
Deploy Microsoft Defender ASR rules starting in audit mode to establish a baseline of legitimate application behavior and identify rules likely to cause false positives in this specific environment, then move high-value rules — block Office applications from creating child processes, block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts, block credential stealing from LSASS, block process creation from PSExec and WMI commands — to block mode on a staged rollout, monitoring Defender ASR audit events (Event ID 1121/1122) throughout. Manage rule deployment centrally via Intune, Group Policy, or Configuration Manager rather than per-device, and review audit telemetry regularly to expand coverage as confidence in the baseline grows.

Executive Recommendation: [COMPANY NAME] should begin the audit-mode rollout within the current quarter given the direct relevance of ASR rules to the phishing-driven attack chains most likely to be used against the organization; full enforcement can follow over subsequent weeks as false positives are tuned out. This is one of the higher-value, lower-cost hardening investments available, since it requires no new tooling beyond the already-licensed Defender stack.

title: Insecure Service Permissions
description:
Windows services run under a defined security context and are described by both a Service Control Manager (SCM) access control list and, separately, permissions on the service's binary, configuration registry key, and working directory. When any of these are misconfigured — a service binary writable by a low-privileged group, a service's registry key (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name>) modifiable by non-administrators, or the SCM ACL itself granting SERVICE_CHANGE_CONFIG or SERVICE_ALL_ACCESS too broadly — a low-privileged local user can redirect what the service executes. If the service runs as SYSTEM or another privileged account, an attacker can replace the target binary or modify the ImagePath registry value to point to an attacker-controlled executable, then restart or wait for the service to run, achieving privilege escalation from a standard user to SYSTEM. Tools such as PowerUp, WinPEAS, and accesschk are standard reconnaissance tools for identifying exactly this class of weak service configuration during both legitimate assessments and real intrusions.

Business Impact: This finding provides a direct, well-documented local privilege escalation path for [CLIENT NAME] — any attacker (or malicious insider) who gains even minimal, low-privileged code execution on an affected host can use it to obtain full SYSTEM control, bypassing whatever access restrictions were intended to limit their impact. It is a common escalation technique observed in real intrusions immediately following an initial low-privilege foothold such as a phishing payload or exposed low-privilege service.
remediation:
Audit service binary, directory, and registry ACLs across the environment using a tool such as accesschk.exe (accesschk.exe -uwcqv <group> *) or PowerUp's Get-ModifiableServiceFile / Get-ModifiableService, and remove write access for any non-administrative principal from service executables, their containing directories, and the corresponding registry keys under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services. Correct SCM-level permissions with sc sdset or the Services MMC snap-in's security tab so that only administrators can reconfigure the service's binary path or start account, and apply this review to any third-party software installers, which are a common source of these misconfigurations.

Executive Recommendation: This should be prioritized as a near-term fix and folded into standard endpoint hardening baselines, since misconfigured service permissions are frequently reintroduced by new software installs rather than being a one-time fix. [COMPANY NAME] should incorporate an automated service-permission check into its endpoint build and patch validation process to prevent regression.

title: Unquoted Service Path
description:
When a Windows service's executable path contains spaces and is not enclosed in quotation marks (for example C:\Program Files\Vendor App\service.exe rather than "C:\Program Files\Vendor App\service.exe"), the Windows service control manager attempts to resolve the path by testing each space-delimited segment as a potential executable in sequence — first C:\Program.exe, then C:\Program Files\Vendor.exe, and so on — before falling back to the full intended path. If an attacker can write a file to any of these intermediate locations (commonly C:\ or C:\Program Files\ itself, where permissions are occasionally looser than expected, or a subdirectory the attacker otherwise controls), planting a malicious executable named to match one of these ambiguous segments causes it to run instead of the legitimate service binary, under whatever privilege level the service is configured to use — frequently SYSTEM.

Business Impact: While this issue requires a writable location along the ambiguous path, when combined with any directory permission weakness it gives an attacker on [CLIENT NAME]'s network a straightforward, well-documented privilege escalation route from a low-privileged foothold to SYSTEM-level control, and it is a standard check performed by both attacker toolkits (WinPEAS, PowerUp) and legitimate red team engagements alike because it is common in environments with a mix of vendor-installed software.
remediation:
Identify all unquoted service paths containing spaces using wmic service get name,pathname,displayname,startmode combined with a filter for unquoted entries, or automated tooling such as PowerUp's Get-UnquotedService, and correct each ImagePath registry value under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<name> to wrap the executable path in quotation marks. Where the vulnerable service was installed by third-party software, verify whether an updated installer resolves the issue, since manually correcting the registry value may be overwritten on the next update or reinstall. As a defense-in-depth measure, verify that C:\ and other top-level directories along common ambiguous paths are not writable by non-administrative users.

Executive Recommendation: This is a quick, scriptable fix that [COMPANY NAME] can resolve environment-wide in a single remediation pass without service disruption, and it should be added to the standard server-build hardening checklist so it does not recur with future software deployments.

title: Domain Admin Logon to Workstations
description:
When accounts with Domain Admin or other Tier 0 privileges authenticate interactively — or even via RDP, PSExec, or scheduled tasks — to standard end-user workstations, their credential material becomes exposed to whatever risk that lower-trust system carries. Standard workstations run user-installed software, are the primary target of phishing, and are far more likely to be compromised than a hardened domain controller or dedicated administrative host; once a privileged account authenticates to such a machine, its NTLM hash, Kerberos tickets, or (absent Credential Guard) plaintext credentials become available in LSASS memory to any attacker who has, or subsequently gains, local administrator rights there. This is precisely the mechanism the Microsoft tiered administration model was designed to prevent, and it is one of the most common escalation paths identified by BloodHound-driven attack path analysis during internal assessments — a workstation compromise combined with a single logged-on Domain Admin session represents a near-immediate path to full domain compromise via Mimikatz-style credential extraction or pass-the-hash.

Business Impact: This finding collapses the separation between everyday endpoint risk and the organization's most sensitive credentials — for [CLIENT NAME], it means that a single phished or malware-infected workstation, ordinarily a contained incident, can become a full domain compromise if a Domain Admin has ever logged onto that machine. This dramatically shortens the realistic timeline from initial foothold to catastrophic, organization-wide impact, and is consistently one of the fastest paths to full compromise observed in internal penetration tests.
remediation:
Implement a tiered administration model (Microsoft's Enhanced Security Admin Environment / tiered model) that strictly separates Tier 0 (domain controllers, PKI, identity infrastructure), Tier 1 (servers), and Tier 2 (workstations) administrative credentials, ensuring Domain Admin and other Tier 0 accounts are never used to log onto Tier 2 workstations under any circumstances. Enforce this technically, not just procedurally, using Group Policy logon restrictions (Deny log on locally / Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services for privileged groups on workstation OUs) and Authentication Policy Silos in newer AD environments, and require administrators to use dedicated Privileged Access Workstations (PAWs) for any Tier 0 activity. Provide administrators with separate standard-privilege accounts for day-to-day work such as email and web browsing.

Executive Recommendation: Given how directly this shortens the path to full domain compromise, [COMPANY NAME] should prioritize deploying logon restrictions for Tier 0 accounts within the current quarter as a foundational identity control, even if the full PAW and tiering rollout takes longer to complete — the technical logon restriction alone closes the most acute exposure at comparatively low implementation cost.

title: Insecure Group Policy Configuration
description:
Group Policy Objects (GPOs) are the primary mechanism for enforcing security baselines, software deployment, and configuration standards across a Windows domain, which also makes them a high-value target: a misconfigured GPO can silently weaken security across every system it applies to, and a GPO with excessive edit or link permissions can be modified by a lower-privileged user to push malicious configuration or code domain-wide. Common findings include GPOs that grant users unintended local administrator rights, disable security controls covered elsewhere in this report (Defender, execution policy, RDP restrictions), embed credentials in scripts or Group Policy Preferences (a legacy technique that stored reversibly-encrypted passwords in SYSVOL, still discoverable years after Microsoft's fix via tools like Get-GPPPassword), or carry weak ACLs that allow non-administrative accounts to edit, link, or modify GPO content. An attacker with write access to a GPO applied to servers or domain controllers can use it to deploy a malicious logon script or scheduled task, achieving code execution as SYSTEM across every machine the GPO touches, an escalation technique commonly enumerated via BloodHound's GPO-edit-rights analysis.

Business Impact: Because GPOs apply configuration at scale, a single insecure GPO can undermine security controls across hundreds of systems simultaneously, or — if its permissions are weak — hand an attacker a mechanism to push malicious code across [CLIENT NAME]'s entire server or workstation fleet in one action. This makes GPO integrity a force-multiplier risk: a flaw here doesn't just affect one system, it can quietly erode the effectiveness of every other hardening control described in this report.
remediation:
Audit all GPOs for excessive edit, link, and delete permissions using the Group Policy Management Console's delegation view or PowerShell (Get-GPO combined with Get-Acl), restricting modification rights to a small, dedicated group of identity administrators. Search SYSVOL and existing GPOs for legacy Group Policy Preferences credentials and remove any found, replacing the underlying use case with Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) or LAPS as appropriate. Review GPO content itself against the organization's security baseline (e.g., Microsoft's Security Compliance Toolkit or CIS Benchmarks) to identify settings that weaken or contradict intended hardening, and establish a change-review process for future GPO edits given their blast radius.

Executive Recommendation: [COMPANY NAME] should prioritize the SYSVOL credential search and GPO permission audit as near-term items given how directly a compromised GPO can undermine every other control in this report, then fold ongoing GPO review into a recurring quarterly cadence owned by the identity/infrastructure team rather than treating it as a one-time cleanup.

title: SMB Signing Disabled
description:
SMB signing cryptographically signs each SMB packet exchanged between client and server, allowing the receiving side to detect tampering or injection. Without it enforced, SMB traffic — including authentication exchanges — can be intercepted and relayed by an attacker positioned on the network path, most commonly via a coerced authentication attack: tools such as Responder poison LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS broadcast requests to capture or redirect authentication attempts, and ntlmrelayx relays the intercepted NTLM authentication in real time to a target server that both accepts NTLM and does not enforce SMB signing, executing actions — including dumping SAM hashes, deploying files, or authenticating to other services — with the relayed victim's privileges rather than the attacker's own. Because this technique requires no cracking of any password, only the ability to observe or coerce authentication traffic, it remains one of the most reliable internal network attack paths and is a near-universal early step in internal penetration tests and real intrusions alike.

Business Impact: SMB relay attacks routinely turn a foothold on any single internal segment of [CLIENT NAME]'s network into administrative access on a specific target server, particularly when a coerced high-privilege account (such as a service account or, worse, a domain controller's own machine account) is relayed. This is frequently the pivot point that converts a contained low-privilege compromise into domain-wide administrative access, and because the technique exploits protocol trust rather than a specific unpatched vulnerability, it persists until signing is enforced rather than being resolved by routine patching.
remediation:
Enforce SMB signing as required (not merely enabled) on all domain controllers and, ideally, all servers and workstations via Group Policy (Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always) and the corresponding client-side setting), rather than leaving it in the negotiated/optional state where an attacker can simply not offer signing to bypass it. Prioritize domain controllers and servers holding sensitive data first if a phased rollout is required, since these are the highest-value relay targets, and validate compatibility with legacy applications before full enforcement, as SMB signing can introduce a measurable performance overhead on high-throughput file servers. This control should be paired with disabling NTLM where feasible and enforcing LDAP signing, since relay attacks pivot across whichever unsigned protocol is available.

Executive Recommendation: Given how directly SMB relay converts a minor foothold into serious compromise, [COMPANY NAME] should enforce signing on domain controllers within days and complete the broader server/workstation rollout within the current quarter — this is a configuration change, not a re-architecture, and its cost is negligible next to the domain-admin-level compromise it prevents.

title: LDAP Signing Not Enforced
description:
LDAP is the protocol domain controllers use to service directory queries and bind requests, and by default Active Directory accepts LDAP binds without requiring signing or channel binding, meaning both the query traffic and the authentication exchange itself can travel unsigned and, in the case of simple binds, potentially in cleartext. This exposes the same relay risk as unsigned SMB: an attacker who coerces or intercepts NTLM authentication over LDAP — for example by relaying a captured machine account authentication to a domain controller's LDAP service with ntlmrelayx — can use the relayed session to perform privileged directory operations, including in well-documented chains adding a computer account (exploiting the default ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota) and then granting that account resource-based constrained delegation rights, or directly modifying attributes to escalate privileges. LDAP channel binding closes a related bypass where TLS-wrapped LDAP (LDAPS) connections could still be relayed if the underlying channel wasn't cryptographically bound to the authentication.

Business Impact: This finding is one of the more direct paths from a network-level foothold to domain compromise for [CLIENT NAME], since LDAP relay attacks against domain controllers can, in several well-documented chains, result in an attacker obtaining privileges equivalent to Domain Admin without ever needing valid domain credentials of their own. Because Active Directory underpins authentication and authorization for essentially every business system, a successful chain here has organization-wide consequences rather than affecting a single application or server.
remediation:
Enforce LDAP signing on all domain controllers via the Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements policy set to Require signing, and enable LDAP channel binding (LdapEnforceChannelBinding registry setting, or the equivalent GPO once available) to close the LDAPS relay bypass. Combine this with SMB signing enforcement and NTLM restriction, since these protections are complementary — an attacker will pivot to whichever protocol remains unsigned. Test the change against any legacy applications or network appliances that perform unsigned LDAP binds before full enforcement, since Microsoft's own guidance notes this as the primary source of compatibility issues.

Executive Recommendation: This should be treated as a priority identity-infrastructure fix and scheduled within the current remediation cycle given its direct role in credential-relay-to-domain-compromise chains; [COMPANY NAME] should assign the domain controller owner to complete a compatibility test and enforce signing across all DCs within a defined, short timeline rather than leaving it in the default optional state indefinitely.

title: Weak Password Policy (Active Directory)
description:
Active Directory's default fine-grained or domain-wide password policy governs minimum length, complexity, history, and lockout thresholds, and when configured too permissively — short minimum length, no meaningful lockout threshold, or complexity requirements that still permit predictable patterns such as Season+Year — it directly enables both online and offline password attacks. Weak lockout configuration in particular enables low-and-slow password spraying, where an attacker attempts a small number of common or seasonal passwords against every account in the directory (rather than many attempts against one account) using tools such as Kerbrute or a custom LDAP/Kerberos bind loop, deliberately staying under the lockout threshold while still achieving a meaningful success rate given how commonly users reuse predictable password patterns across an organization. Short or weakly-complex passwords additionally reduce the offline cracking time for any hash obtained via Kerberoasting, NTDS.dit extraction, or credential dumping, compounding the impact of several other findings in this report.

Business Impact: Weak password policy rarely causes a breach in isolation, but it is a force-multiplier that increases the success rate and speed of nearly every other attack technique observed in an internal assessment of [CLIENT NAME]'s environment — from password spraying against externally exposed services to offline cracking of hashes obtained through other means. Because a successful spray or crack against even one account can be the initial foothold for a much larger compromise, this finding materially raises the likelihood that other, more severe findings in this report become practically exploitable rather than theoretical.
remediation:
Adopt current NIST 800-63B-aligned guidance rather than legacy complexity rules: enforce a longer minimum password length (14+ characters, ideally passphrase-based) rather than relying on complexity composition rules alone, implement a reasonable account lockout threshold with automatic reset, and deploy Azure AD Password Protection or a third-party breached-password/dictionary check to block common and previously-compromised passwords at set time. Prioritize multi-factor authentication for all remote-access and privileged accounts as the primary mitigation against password-based compromise, since password policy alone cannot fully prevent spraying or credential stuffing using externally breached credentials. Use fine-grained password policies to apply stricter requirements to privileged and service accounts specifically.

Executive Recommendation: [COMPANY NAME] should treat MFA deployment for remote access and privileged accounts as the higher-priority near-term action, with password policy modernization following as a broader identity project — together these substantially reduce the practical success rate of the credential attacks that underpin many of the other findings in this report, making this a high-leverage area for security investment.

title: Excessive Privileged Group Membership
description:
Active Directory's built-in privileged groups — Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins, Account Operators, Backup Operators, and similar — grant sweeping rights across the domain or forest, and membership in them is frequently found to have grown beyond genuine operational need over time as accounts are added for one-off tasks and never removed. Every member of these groups represents an equally attractive target for an attacker performing privilege-escalation reconnaissance, typically via BloodHound, which maps group membership and derived attack paths across the domain; a larger privileged group simply multiplies the number of accounts an attacker can target for credential theft, phishing, or exploitation of that specific user's endpoint to obtain the same domain-wide privileges as a dedicated, well-protected administrator account would carry. Some built-in groups (Account Operators, Backup Operators) carry privileges that are frequently overlooked as effectively equivalent to Domain Admin, since they can reset passwords on privileged accounts or access the raw NTDS.dit database, respectively.

Business Impact: Every unnecessary member of a privileged group is an additional attack surface for [CLIENT NAME]'s most sensitive access — instead of an attacker needing to compromise one well-protected administrator, they can succeed by compromising any one of a much larger set of ordinary users who happen to carry excess privilege, often without those users even being aware of the risk their account represents. Reducing this group down to genuine need is one of the most cost-effective ways to shrink the domain's overall attack surface, since it requires no new tooling, only disciplined access review.
remediation:
Conduct a full audit of all AD privileged groups — Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins, Account Operators, Backup Operators, Server Operators, and any custom groups delegated significant rights — and remove membership that is not tied to an active, documented operational need, using BloodHound or PowerShell (Get-ADGroupMember) to enumerate current membership and nested group paths that may grant privilege indirectly. Establish a recurring quarterly access review as a standing process, since privileged group membership tends to grow again without one, and implement Just-In-Time privileged access (via Privileged Access Management or time-bound group membership) so that administrative rights are granted only for the duration of the task requiring them rather than standing permanently.

Executive Recommendation: [COMPANY NAME] should complete an initial cleanup of privileged group membership within the current quarter and establish the recurring review as an ongoing governance process owned by identity/security operations — this is a low-cost, high-impact control, and its absence is one of the most common findings BloodHound-driven attack path analysis surfaces during penetration tests, making it a frequent, low-effort route to full domain compromise if left unaddressed.

title: Kerberoasting Exposure
description:
Any authenticated domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket for any service that has a registered Service Principal Name (SPN), and that ticket is encrypted using a key derived from the target service account's own password hash (RC4 or AES, depending on configuration). Because any domain user — not just an administrator — can request this ticket without triggering any special privilege check, an attacker with even a low-privileged foothold can enumerate SPN-registered accounts using tools like PowerView, Rubeus, or Impacket's GetUserSPNs.py, request service tickets for all of them, and take the encrypted portion offline for password cracking with hashcat, entirely outside the visibility and lockout protection of the domain controller. Because service accounts are frequently provisioned once and never revisited, their passwords are disproportionately likely to be old, weak, or unchanged since creation, and — critically — service accounts are also disproportionately likely to hold elevated or unusual privileges (local admin on multiple servers, membership in privileged groups) compared to ordinary user accounts.
