Business Impact: A weak visitor process converts every plausible pretext — a fake delivery, a fake interview, a fake service call — into a viable path onto [CLIENT NAME]'s premises, from which an attacker can conduct reconnaissance, photograph sensitive material, plant a rogue device, or simply walk out with an unattended laptop. This finding is frequently the first step in a broader social-engineering attack chain, since physical presence lends an attacker legitimacy for follow-on actions like impersonating IT staff or accessing supposedly restricted areas.
remediation:
Implement mandatory visitor sign-in capturing identity, host, purpose, and time of arrival/departure, issue a visually distinct temporary badge for every visitor, and require an escort for any visitor moving beyond a designated public reception area. Train reception and front-line staff to challenge unbadged individuals politely but consistently, and reinforce through periodic security awareness communication that this is expected behavior rather than something that risks offending a legitimate guest. Review visitor logs periodically to confirm the process is actually being followed, not just documented in policy.

Executive Recommendation: This is a low-cost, process-driven fix that [COMPANY NAME] can implement within a few weeks using existing reception staff and off-the-shelf visitor management tools. Given how often physical access enables broader social-engineering attacks, closing this gap should be treated as a meaningful risk-reduction step relative to its minimal implementation cost.

title: Tailgating Exposure
description:
Tailgating occurs when an unauthorized individual follows an authorized employee through a badge-controlled door without presenting their own credential — exploiting normal social courtesy (holding a door open) rather than any technical flaw in the access control system itself. During a physical penetration test, this is demonstrated by an assessor approaching a secured entrance carrying a plausible prop (a box, a coffee tray, a laptop bag) and simply following an employee through the door; in most organizations without specific anti-tailgating training or controls, employees hold the door rather than challenge an unfamiliar person, particularly when the individual appears busy, confident, or dressed appropriately for the environment.

This single technique routinely defeats an otherwise well-implemented badge access system, since the electronic control only verifies the credential of the person who badges in, not everyone who physically passes through the door behind them.

Business Impact: Tailgating is one of the most reliable techniques in a physical red-team engagement precisely because it targets human behavior rather than the access control technology, meaning [CLIENT NAME]'s investment in badge readers and door hardware provides little protection if staff aren't trained and empowered to challenge followers. Once inside, an attacker gains the same physical proximity to systems, documents, and unattended workstations as any legitimate employee, making this a common entry point for broader social-engineering or data-theft scenarios.
remediation:
Deploy physical anti-tailgating controls where the risk justifies the cost — mantrap-style doors, turnstiles, or door sensors that alert on multiple entries per badge — at the highest-sensitivity entry points, and combine this with security awareness training that explicitly authorizes and encourages employees to politely challenge unbadged individuals following them through a door. Reinforce the expected behavior through periodic unannounced tailgating tests (with results shared as coaching, not punishment) so the training translates into practiced behavior rather than a one-time policy memo. Post visible signage at controlled entrances reminding staff that one badge equals one person through the door.

Executive Recommendation: Prioritize the awareness-training component immediately, since it is inexpensive and addresses the majority of the risk; treat physical mantrap hardware as a longer-term investment for the highest-value entry points such as data center or server room access. [COMPANY NAME] should repeat tailgating tests periodically, since this is a behavioral control that decays without reinforcement.

title: Unsecured Workstations
description:
Workstations left unlocked while unattended — whether due to a missing or overly long inactivity timeout, or simply an employee stepping away without manually locking the screen — provide anyone who reaches the desk with the same access as the logged-in user: open email, active VPN or application sessions, saved credentials in a browser, and any file shares or internal tools the user's session already has open. During an on-site physical assessment, this is typically documented simply by walking the floor during breaks or after-hours and noting how many screens are unlocked and accessible, often alongside adjacent findings like visible sticky-note passwords or unattended badge cards left on the desk.

An attacker with even brief physical proximity — a tailgating intruder, a malicious visitor, or an opportunistic insider — can use an unlocked session to install a backdoor, exfiltrate files, send phishing email from the legitimate user's account to other staff, or pivot to internal systems the user has standing access to, all without needing any credentials of their own.

Business Impact: An unattended, unlocked workstation collapses the effort required for account compromise from "steal credentials" to "walk up to a desk," and because the resulting actions occur under a legitimate employee's identity, they are harder for [CLIENT NAME] to detect and attribute after the fact. Where the affected user has elevated access — finance, HR, IT administration — a single unlocked session during a lunch break can be sufficient for meaningful data theft or lateral movement.
remediation:
Enforce an automatic screen lock via Group Policy (Windows) or MDM/configuration profile (macOS) at a short inactivity timeout — typically 2-5 minutes for general staff and shorter for privileged workstations — so the control does not depend on individual habit. Reinforce a clean-desk and lock-when-leaving culture through security awareness training and periodic, unannounced walk-throughs that note (without publicly shaming) unlocked screens, feeding results back into targeted coaching. Consider proximity-based auto-lock (Bluetooth-paired phone or badge) for higher-risk roles where a manual habit is judged insufficient.

Executive Recommendation: This is a same-week fix — a Group Policy/MDM setting change — with essentially no implementation cost, so there is no reason to delay it. [COMPANY NAME] should treat consistent lock-screen enforcement as baseline hygiene that materially reduces the blast radius of any physical intrusion, tailgating incident, or insider scenario already identified elsewhere in this assessment.

title: Sensitive Documents Exposed
description:
Printed material left on desks, in shared printer output trays, or written on whiteboards visible from walkways, windows, or meeting-room glass routinely contains information an organization would not otherwise disclose — network diagrams, credentials scrawled during a troubleshooting session, customer data printed for review, org charts, or strategic planning notes. During a physical assessment, this is documented through simple observation while walking the office: photographing (with client authorization) exposed whiteboards, papers left on desks overnight, or documents sitting uncollected in printer trays, often in areas visible to visitors, cleaning staff, or anyone passing a window.

Because this information requires no technical exploitation to obtain — only proximity and a willingness to look — it is frequently the fastest reconnaissance an attacker or malicious insider can perform, and whiteboard photographs from a single meeting-room walkthrough have, in real engagements, yielded working credentials or internal network details.

Business Impact: Exposed printed and written material bypasses every technical control [CLIENT NAME] has in place, since the information is disclosed directly rather than extracted through a system. A single photographed whiteboard or an uncollected printout containing customer records can constitute a reportable data exposure on its own, and even non-regulated material like network diagrams or credentials meaningfully accelerates a subsequent technical attack by removing the reconnaissance phase entirely.
remediation:
Implement and actively enforce a clean desk policy requiring sensitive documents to be locked away or shredded rather than left on desks at end of day, and configure shared printers with a pull-print/release-code feature so documents only print when the requesting user is physically present to collect them. Position whiteboards containing sensitive discussion content away from windows and visitor sightlines, and require them to be erased after meetings involving credentials, architecture details, or customer information. Reinforce the policy through periodic after-hours walk-throughs with findings fed back to management as a metric, not just a one-time audit.

Executive Recommendation: This is a low-cost, policy-and-behavior fix that [COMPANY NAME] can roll out within weeks alongside existing security awareness training. Given how directly this shortcuts an attacker's reconnaissance effort, it merits equal priority to technical findings despite its non-technical nature.

title: Insecure Media Disposal
description:
Storage media — hard drives, SSDs, backup tapes, USB drives — and printed documents that reach end-of-life are only as secure as their disposal process; media placed in general office trash, recycling, or an unsecured e-waste bin without data destruction remains fully readable to anyone who retrieves it, since deletion or a quick format does not remove data from the underlying storage medium. During a physical assessment, this is commonly identified by inspecting waste and recycling areas (with client authorization) for discarded drives, printed reports, or documents that were never shredded, and in prior real-world engagements, recovered drives and dumpster-retrieved paperwork have yielded readable customer records and credentials with no forensic effort beyond plugging in the drive or reading the page.

This technique, sometimes called dumpster diving, requires no technical skill and is legal to attempt against material placed in publicly accessible waste areas in many jurisdictions, making it a low-risk, low-cost reconnaissance or data-theft method for an attacker.

Business Impact: Improperly disposed media is a direct, non-technical data breach vector for [CLIENT NAME] — recovered drives or documents can expose customer PII, financial records, or credentials with the same regulatory consequences as a network intrusion, since data protection law does not distinguish between a hacked database and an unshredded printout in a dumpster. This is a frequent finding in compliance-driven assessments (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS) precisely because "secure disposal" is an explicit, auditable control requirement in most of these frameworks.
remediation:
Establish a certified media destruction process — cross-cut shredding for paper, and degaussing or physical destruction (not just deletion or reformatting) for hard drives, SSDs, and other electronic storage — using a vendor who provides a certificate of destruction for audit purposes. Deploy secure, locked shredding bins throughout the office for interim document collection rather than relying on staff to walk documents to a central shredder, and maintain a chain-of-custody log for decommissioned hardware from collection through destruction. Include disposal procedures explicitly in the IT asset lifecycle and offboarding processes so no device leaves custody without going through them.

Executive Recommendation: Address this promptly, particularly if any customer or financial data has recently left the building through untracked disposal, since [COMPANY NAME] cannot rule out prior exposure without reviewing recent disposal practices. A certified destruction vendor contract is a modest recurring cost relative to the regulatory and reputational cost of a disposal-related breach notification.

title: Missing CCTV Monitoring
description:
The absence of camera coverage at sensitive locations — building entrances, server rooms, loading docks, and areas storing physical assets — removes both a deterrent against unauthorized access and the forensic record needed to investigate an incident after the fact. During a physical assessment, this gap is identified simply by surveying the premises for camera placement and coverage angles, and it is frequently found alongside other physical findings in this report: an unrestricted server room or a tailgating-prone entrance without any corresponding camera coverage means those incidents, if they occurred, would leave no evidence to review.

Without footage, an organization investigating a suspected physical intrusion, device theft, or unauthorized after-hours access has no independent way to confirm what happened, who was involved, or whether other areas were also affected, and it cannot support any subsequent law enforcement or insurance claim with objective evidence.

Business Impact: Missing CCTV coverage compounds every other physical finding in this assessment, since it means [CLIENT NAME] would have no way to determine after an incident whether a server room breach, device theft, or tailgating event actually led to compromise, or to identify the individual responsible. Beyond incident response, the lack of visible camera coverage also reduces the deterrent effect that discourages opportunistic physical intrusion attempts in the first place.
remediation:
Deploy CCTV coverage at all critical access points — main entrances, server rooms, network closets, loading docks, and any area storing high-value or sensitive physical assets — with camera placement reviewed to eliminate blind spots at points of entry. Set a retention policy for recorded footage aligned with the organization's incident response and compliance needs (commonly 30-90 days), store recordings on a system separate from the general network to prevent tampering by an attacker who gains network access, and restrict footage access and export to authorized security personnel. Combine visible cameras with signage, since visible coverage itself carries deterrent value independent of the recording.

Executive Recommendation: Treat this as a near-term investment, particularly for locations flagged elsewhere in this assessment as having weak access controls, since camera coverage is what turns those findings from unverifiable risk into an investigable, actionable incident if exploited. [COMPANY NAME] should budget for coverage as part of a broader physical security uplift rather than deferring it indefinitely, given the comparatively low hardware cost relative to the value of being able to investigate a real incident.

title: Unsecured Network Ports
description:
Active, unauthenticated network ports in publicly reachable or uncontrolled areas — lobby waiting areas, unlocked conference rooms, unused offices, or wall jacks behind furniture — allow anyone who can physically reach the jack to plug in a laptop or a small implant device (a Raspberry Pi or similar) and gain a foothold directly on the internal network, bypassing perimeter firewalls and any network-edge controls entirely. During a physical/internal assessment, this is confirmed by connecting a test device to an accessible port and checking whether it receives a DHCP lease with meaningful internal network access, or whether internal-only services and hosts become reachable — commonly demonstrated by capturing broadcast traffic with a tool like Wireshark or Responder to confirm exposure to internal protocols such as NetBIOS/LLMNR.

A network implant left in an inconspicuous location can also provide an attacker persistent remote access to the internal network well after they've physically left the building, if it includes its own cellular or Wi-Fi uplink.

Business Impact: An unsecured port in a lobby or unlocked meeting room gives an attacker the same starting position as a malicious insider sitting at a desk, without requiring them to compromise any credentials or bypass any perimeter defense — a significant escalation from the outside-in access most of [CLIENT NAME]'s security investment is designed to resist. This is a common and realistic finding in social-engineering-driven physical assessments, since a visitor or contractor left briefly unattended in a conference room is a plausible, low-suspicion scenario.
remediation:
Implement 802.1X network access control (NAC) so that any device plugged into a wall port must authenticate before receiving meaningful network access, rather than being placed directly on the internal VLAN by default. Where full NAC deployment is a longer-term project, apply interim compensating controls: disable switch ports not actively assigned to a known device, place publicly accessible ports (lobbies, unlocked meeting rooms) on an isolated guest VLAN with no access to internal resources, and physically secure or remove unused wall jacks in uncontrolled areas. Periodically audit active switch ports against expected device inventory to catch drift.

Executive Recommendation: Treat guest-area port isolation as an immediate, low-effort fix, and scope full 802.1X NAC deployment as a medium-term project given its broader infrastructure impact. [COMPANY NAME] should weigh the NAC investment against the fact that this finding, if exploited, grants an attacker internal network position directly — a foothold that would otherwise typically require a successful phishing or external compromise to obtain.

title: Device Theft Exposure
description:
Laptops, external drives, and other portable devices that leave the office in bags, on desks near windows, or unattended in vehicles are exposed to opportunistic and targeted theft, and the security consequence of that theft depends almost entirely on whether the device's storage is encrypted. An unencrypted or weakly protected device recovered by a thief can be booted from external media or have its drive removed and read directly on another machine, bypassing the OS login screen entirely and exposing every file, cached credential, and locally stored document on the device. During an assessment, this is evaluated by checking whether full-disk encryption (BitLocker, FileVault) is enabled and enforced fleet-wide, and by observing physical theft-prevention practices such as unattended laptops in open workspaces, vehicles, or public areas without a cable lock or comparable control.

Business Impact: Device theft is one of the most common real-world loss scenarios organizations face, and without full-disk encryption, a single stolen laptop becomes a full data breach rather than a hardware replacement cost for [CLIENT NAME] — with the exact severity depending on what the departing employee's laptop happened to have cached locally at the time. Regulatory breach-notification obligations under GDPR and similar frameworks generally apply to unencrypted device loss but do not apply, or apply with far less severity, when full-disk encryption can be demonstrated to have been active, making encryption both a practical and a compliance-relevant control.
remediation:
Enforce full-disk encryption (BitLocker with TPM-backed key protection on Windows, FileVault on macOS) fleet-wide via MDM policy, with encryption status monitored centrally so unencrypted devices are flagged and remediated automatically rather than relying on individual compliance. Deploy cable locks for devices regularly left in shared or semi-public workspaces, and reinforce through policy and training that devices should never be left visible in vehicles or unattended in public areas. Enable remote-wipe capability through the MDM platform so a reported theft or loss can trigger immediate data destruction where the device later connects to a network.

Executive Recommendation: Confirm and close any gaps in full-disk encryption coverage immediately, since it is inexpensive to enable and is the single control that most changes the consequence of an inevitable lost or stolen device. [COMPANY NAME] should treat encryption compliance as a standing MDM metric reported to security leadership, not a one-time rollout, since new devices and exceptions accumulate over time.

title: Hardware Tampering Risk
description:
Critical hardware — network switches, servers, kiosks, point-of-sale terminals, or peripherals like keyboards in publicly accessible areas — that lacks tamper-evident seals, regular physical inspection, or a documented chain of custody creates an opportunity for an attacker with brief physical access to install a hardware implant without detection. Common real-world examples include a hardware keylogger inserted between a keyboard and its USB port, a small network tap or Wi-Fi-enabled implant connected inline on a switch, or a skimming device attached to a payment terminal — all of which can be installed in under a minute by someone posing as maintenance staff, a cleaner, or simply left briefly unsupervised near the equipment. During a physical assessment, this risk is evaluated by inspecting cable runs, USB ports, and equipment enclosures for unauthorized devices and by checking whether any tamper-evident mechanism or inspection process exists to detect this kind of modification.

Business Impact: A hardware implant is particularly dangerous because it typically bypasses every network- and endpoint-based security control [CLIENT NAME] has deployed, operating below the layer those tools monitor, and can persist for months collecting credentials or traffic before discovery, if it is ever discovered at all. For payment-processing equipment specifically, an undetected skimming implant carries direct PCI-DSS and card-brand liability exposure in addition to the underlying fraud loss.
remediation:
Apply tamper-evident seals to equipment enclosures, cable connections, and USB ports on critical or publicly accessible hardware, and establish a routine, documented physical inspection schedule (e.g., during regular IT maintenance) specifically looking for seal breaks, unfamiliar inline devices, or altered cabling. Restrict physical access to critical equipment locations per the access-control recommendations elsewhere in this assessment, since inspection is a detective control and access restriction remains the primary preventive one. For payment terminals specifically, follow PCI-DSS-mandated device inspection procedures and maintain a hardware inventory with serial numbers to detect unauthorized substitution.

Executive Recommendation: Implement tamper-evident controls and an inspection schedule within the next quarter, prioritizing payment terminals and network infrastructure given the direct fraud and confidentiality impact of an undetected implant. [COMPANY NAME] should view this as a modest, low-cost addition to existing maintenance routines rather than a new standalone program, since the marginal effort of a visual tamper check is small relative to the cost of an undetected hardware compromise.

title: Missing Immutable Backup Policy Protections
description:
Backup archives stored on standard read-write volumes or shares remain fully subject to modification and deletion by any identity with sufficient privilege on the backup system or the network path leading to it, with no cryptographic or storage-enforced guarantee against overwrite. This matters specifically because ransomware operators have, for several years, treated backup destruction as a core phase of the attack rather than an afterthought: once an actor obtains domain admin or equivalent credentials through the primary network (commonly via Kerberoasting, credential dumping with Mimikatz, or lateral movement following an initial phishing foothold), they routinely enumerate and target backup infrastructure specifically, deleting Volume Shadow Copies (vssadmin delete shadows), disabling backup jobs, or directly encrypting the backup repository itself before detonating ransomware on production systems — ensuring the victim organization cannot simply restore its way out of the incident.

Because the backup system typically trusts the same administrative identities as the production environment, a single compromised domain admin credential is often sufficient to reach and destroy both the primary data and its recovery copies in the same operation.

Business Impact: Without immutability, [CLIENT NAME]'s backups provide a false sense of resilience — they exist and pass routine restore tests, but offer no actual protection against the specific attack (ransomware with credential compromise) they are most needed for. This transforms what could be a contained, restorable ransomware incident into an extended outage with no clean recovery point, materially increasing the pressure to pay a ransom and extending downtime, both of which carry direct financial and, for regulated data, breach-notification consequences under frameworks like GDPR or sector-specific continuity requirements.
remediation:
Migrate backup storage to a platform enforcing true immutability — WORM-capable storage arrays, or cloud Object Lock in compliance mode (not governance mode, which privileged accounts can still override) on S3 or equivalent object storage — with a defined retention window during which no identity, including backup administrators, can modify or delete stored backups. As an interim or complementary control, maintain an offline or air-gapped backup copy that is never continuously network-reachable from the production domain, and enforce a separate administrative identity and credential set for the backup platform that is not part of the same Active Directory trust as production systems. Regularly test restoration from the immutable copy specifically, not just from the live backup set, to confirm the protection holds under real recovery conditions.

Executive Recommendation: This should be treated as a high-priority item given the direct role backup destruction plays in modern ransomware attacks — schedule the migration within the current quarter rather than as a longer-term roadmap item. [COMPANY NAME] should weigh the modest cost of Object Lock or WORM storage against the alternative of negotiating a ransom or rebuilding from nothing, a comparison that consistently favors upfront investment in immutability.

title: Publicly Accessible Backup Storage Infrastructure
description:
Backup servers, management consoles, and the network paths leading to them are frequently treated as internal-only infrastructure and, as a result, are sometimes left reachable directly from the internet or from broad internal network segments without dedicated network isolation — a gap that is easy to introduce during initial setup or a cloud migration and easy to overlook afterward, since backup systems rarely appear in the same asset inventories or vulnerability scanning scope as production applications. An external attacker can locate these exposed services through routine internet-wide scanning (Shodan, Censys, or a targeted nmap sweep against the organization's IP ranges) and, once identified, attempt credential stuffing against the login portal, exploit known unpatched vulnerabilities in the backup software itself (backup platforms including Veeam, Commvault, and others have had high-severity remote-exploitation CVEs in recent years), or pivot from an internal but unsegmented network position with no additional authentication barrier.

Because backup platforms typically hold privileged, domain-trusted service accounts to reach the systems they back up, compromising the backup console itself is often a faster path to broad access than attacking production systems directly.

Business Impact: An exposed backup console is disproportionately valuable to an attacker relative to its visibility in most organizations' security programs — successful compromise can expose [CLIENT NAME]'s complete historical data footprint in a single location, and the backup platform's typically broad service-account privileges make it an efficient stepping stone into the wider environment. Because backup infrastructure is under-monitored relative to production systems in many organizations, an intrusion through this path can also go undetected substantially longer than one through a more heavily monitored front door.
remediation:
Move backup management interfaces and their underlying network paths onto a dedicated, firewalled management network with no direct internet exposure and only least-privilege routing from the segments that specifically need to reach it, verified with an external port scan to confirm nothing remains publicly reachable. Require high-assurance multi-factor authentication for all backup console access, apply vendor security patches on an accelerated timeline given the platform's track record of high-severity CVEs, and use a dedicated, non-domain-trusted service account for the backup platform's access to production systems where the backup architecture allows it, so a backup compromise does not automatically yield domain-wide access. Include backup infrastructure explicitly in regular vulnerability scanning and asset inventory scope, since its exclusion is a common and consequential gap.

Executive Recommendation: Remediate internet-facing exposure immediately — this is a same-week fix given the low effort of a firewall rule change relative to the severity of the exposure. [COMPANY NAME] should also commission a broader review of what other management infrastructure may have similarly fallen outside standard asset inventory and patching processes, since backup systems are rarely an isolated instance of this pattern.

title: Insecure Encryption of Backup Data at Rest
description:
Backup jobs that write full system configurations, database dumps, and file-level copies to storage without encryption produce, by design, a complete and highly consolidated copy of the organization's sensitive data in cleartext — arguably a more attractive target than any single production system, since one backup set can contain what would otherwise require compromising many separate systems to assemble. This exposure materializes through several realistic paths: physical theft or improper disposal of backup media or decommissioned storage hardware, interception of backup replication traffic on an internal network segment (trivial to capture with a tool like Wireshark if the transport itself is also unencrypted), or unauthorized access to a cloud storage bucket or file share hosting backup archives — a scenario made materially worse by cloud storage misconfigurations, which regularly appear in this assessment's broader findings.

Because the data is unencrypted, none of these access paths require breaking any cryptographic protection; recovering the underlying data is a matter of reading the file directly.

Business Impact: Unencrypted backups mean that any single point of physical or logical access to the backup storage layer — rather than to production systems individually — yields [CLIENT NAME]'s complete data footprint at once, disproportionately amplifying the impact of what might otherwise be a contained storage misconfiguration or a single stolen drive. Where those backups include customer PII, payment data, or health records, this creates the same GDPR, PCI-DSS, or HIPAA breach-notification exposure as a production database compromise, but originating from infrastructure that is frequently reviewed and monitored less rigorously than the production systems it protects.
remediation:
Enable AES-256 encryption at rest for all backup repositories, whether on-premises storage arrays, tape, or cloud object storage, using the backup platform's native encryption capability or storage-layer encryption (e.g., cloud provider server-side encryption with customer-managed keys) rather than leaving data unencrypted by default. Store and manage encryption keys separately from the backup data itself — in a dedicated hardware security module or cloud KMS with restricted access policies and key rotation — so that compromise of the storage layer alone does not also yield the decryption key. Extend the same protection to backup data in transit (TLS for replication traffic) and verify encryption status as part of routine backup job monitoring, not just at initial configuration.

Executive Recommendation: Prioritize this fix within the current quarter given the concentrated impact of a single unencrypted backup set relative to individual production system exposures. [COMPANY NAME] should treat backup encryption and key management as a standing compliance control subject to periodic verification, since a lapsed or misconfigured key rotation can silently undermine the protection long after initial rollout.

title: Insecure OAuth Redirect URI / Custom URL Scheme Handling
description:
Mobile OAuth 2.0 implementations that rely on a custom URL scheme (e.g., myapp://) to receive the authorization code or access token back from the identity provider face an inherent platform limitation: unlike a web origin, a custom URL scheme is not exclusively ownable. Both Android and iOS historically allowed any installed application to register the same custom scheme, and on Android specifically, multiple apps can declare an identical intent-filter scheme with no OS-level conflict resolution guaranteeing delivery to the intended app — the system may present a chooser, or in some configurations silently deliver the callback to whichever app was installed or granted the association first. A malicious application that registers the same scheme as the legitimate app can intercept the OAuth redirect carrying the authorization code (or, in the deprecated but still-encountered implicit flow, the access token directly in the URL fragment) before the legitimate app ever receives it. Compounding this, many implementations fail to validate the redirect_uri strictly against a pre-registered value on the authorization server side, allowing an attacker to register a lookalike or attacker-controlled redirect URI during the OAuth flow itself and have the authorization code delivered directly to infrastructure they control, no device-level interception required. Once obtained, the intercepted authorization code can typically be exchanged for a full access token, especially where PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) is not enforced, since without PKCE any party in possession of the code can complete the token exchange.

Business Impact: This flaw lets an attacker fully impersonate a legitimate user's session in [CLIENT NAME]'s mobile application without ever needing the user's password, since OAuth-based single sign-on is often explicitly designed to avoid handling credentials directly — turning the redirect handling into the actual point of failure. Because OAuth is frequently used to authenticate against high-value identity providers (corporate SSO, social login tied to payment methods, or partner API access), a successful interception can cascade into access well beyond the mobile app itself, and detection is difficult since the resulting session looks, from the server's perspective, like a normal successful login.
remediation:
Adopt App Links (Android) or Universal Links (iOS) instead of custom URL schemes for the OAuth redirect wherever the identity provider and app configuration support it — these bind the callback to a domain the app owner cryptographically proves ownership of via a hosted well-known file, closing the scheme-squatting interception path entirely. Where a custom scheme cannot be avoided, use a long, unguessable, app-specific scheme rather than a generic one, and mandate PKCE (RFC 7636) on every OAuth flow so that even an intercepted authorization code is useless to an attacker without the original code_verifier, which never leaves the legitimate app instance. On the authorization server side, enforce an exact-match allow-list for registered redirect_uri values — reject partial matches, wildcard subdomains, or open-ended path matching — and ensure the state parameter is validated on return to prevent CSRF-style flow injection alongside the redirect issue.

Executive Recommendation: Treat this as a priority fix for the current release, particularly if the app's OAuth integration protects access to payment functionality, corporate SSO, or sensitive personal data, since PKCE and redirect_uri allow-listing are both well-established, low-effort mitigations relative to the severity of a full account-takeover primitive. [COMPANY NAME] should confirm PKCE enforcement across every OAuth-integrated mobile client, not just the one flagged here, as this is a common gap when OAuth libraries are integrated without security review of their default configuration.
